After playing Total War games from Medieval 2 to Shogun 2 for almost two decades I've decided to finally give a try to the first game of the series. I've seen some videos on first Medieval and this game and I found some of the design choices, such as the map being an actual map, with pawns representing your armies, castles and agents to be appaling enough to try it myself.

So to start of - the campaign map. It's a nice change to operate on the province level instead of running your armies using their movement points. It really forces you to think otherwise about your moves on the campaign map, as provinces often border many others, enemy can attack your lands from different directions - and once they enter, you have to fight them all in one battle, instead of driving them back in different places alongside the border, as it is in the newer titles. The map is kept simple: in order to know anything more about provinces around you, you have to click on them and read the info from a scroll. It's the only way to learn that a province has gold deposits or produces excellent archers. What is definitely different to the later Total Wars is that a province has only one battle map - so if you are fighting a couple of times in the same highland province, you probably are going to place your archers always in the same spot. Every province looks different, but it can become tiresome, if you are fighting numerous times for control of this one province.
I have mixed feelings about battles themselves. On one hand, weather plays a very huge role in how your units perform, just as terrain does - which is a stark difference to later titles, e. g. in Medieval 2 archers don't really care about fog or rain - and I really like this aspect. Correct positioning of your troops is a key factor in securing the victory in this game, as the roster for all clans is the same and their stats don't differ - which leads to the terrain, fatigue of your troops and their honour (experience) to be crucial factors during the battle. I've played on the expert difficulty, so maybe I'm biased, but I don't think that your tactic matters that much, main thing is that you place your troops well, don't make them charge uphill or shoot uphill. Flanking usually doesn't matter, the enemy won't break anyways. Cavalry charges are also quite unspectacular, cavalry is rather useful in catching the enemy - be it fleeing or marching - that your infantry can't reach. A propos cavalry - they suffer the most from the fact that it's difficult in this game to pull your troops out of the fight. As soon as one of the soldiers comes in contact with enemy, the whole unit becomes quite unresponsive (it's especially painful when the enemy sends his daimyo against you, as he is quite invincible and will kill dozens of your men, who can't move away from him). The pathfinding of units is sometimes tiresome, as sometimes ordering units to move forward causes only one "wing" of the unit to come forth, leading the unit to stand with their flank opposing the charging enemy, causing a massive morale penalty. The fact that your (almost) only control is the LMB doesn't help either, I've had numerous situations when I missed a button by a milimeter, so instead of choosing a different unit, I've sent the one previously selected somewhere where I didn't want them to be.
The battle AI is quite satisfying to fight against: it moves cautiosly, looks for the best angle for charge or awaits you in a favourable position if you are the attacker. The fact that it tends to route from battles it finds impossible to win is simultanously its advantage and disadvantage - I really appreciate that it doesn't throw its soldiers mindlessly at you, but saves them for another battle, but it sometimes forgets, that it can't retreat anywhere on the strategic map - causing the whole army to perish in vain.
The game isn't very helpful in explaining how it works. On one hand, when attacking/defending a province, you get a nice tab informing you about all armies involved, number of men taking part and about the options you have: attack/defend, abandon the province/call off the attack, retreat into the castle (which, depending on its size, can house only limited amount of your troops). On the other hand, it doesn't give you any insight into the building tree, never gives any info whether your reinforcements will arrive or not, doesn't calculate the public order immedietely after you move your troops out of the province but only the next turn. There are also some other poor mechanic choices, such as the fact that you can only talk to a clan by sending your emissary to the other daimyo, tough luck if you can't find him on the map because he is on the other side of Japan.
I could also write about other aspects, such as outdated graphics or limited diplomacy options (you either have no dip relations, are in war or have an alliance), but I think this review is long enough. All in all, I wouldn't recommend it for more than one campaign. The battles, the quintesence of the Total War franchise, become quite repetitive really fast and the limitations of this ancient game engine really show. Worth a try only if you're really interested in how the whole series began

A Timeless Strategy Classic

I just finished 100% completing both the main campaign and the Mongol Invasion in Shogun: Total War, The very first!! and I honestly had an absolute blast the entire time.

For a game released in 2000, it still delivers some of the most tense, atmospheric, and rewarding strategy gameplay I’ve experienced. The campaign map is clean and focused, but every decision feels meaningful. Expansion, diplomacy, honour, clan management — it all matters. There’s no bloat, just pure strategic depth.

The battles are where it really shines. Watching lines of yari ashigaru hold the line while samurai crash into combat never gets old. Morale is EVERYTHING in this game, and when a well-timed cavalry charge collapses an enemy flank, it feels earned. It’s slower and more methodical than modern Total War titles, but that’s exactly why it works so well. Positioning, terrain, and timing actually matter.

100%ing the main campaign was incredibly satisfying, but the Shogun: Total War - The Mongol Invasion expansion added a whole new layer of challenge. Facing the Mongol hordes completely changes the pacing — suddenly you’re on the defensive against relentless, high-quality armies. It pushed me to adapt, rethink my strategies, and really master the mechanics. Finishing both campaigns felt like a genuine accomplishment.

There’s also something special about the atmosphere. The music, the UI, the pre-battle speeches — it all creates this grounded, almost meditative samurai-era vibe that newer games sometimes lose in scale.

Even today, this game proves that strong design outlives graphics. If you’re a strategy fan and want to experience where the Total War series began, this is absolutely worth your time.

Shogun: Total War – Collection is a landmark strategy title that still carries remarkable weight decades after its original release. Developed by Creative Assembly and published by SEGA, this collection brings together the base game and its Mongol Invasion expansion, offering the definitive version of the classic that launched the Total War franchise. While the series would eventually evolve into sprawling, mechanically dense epics, Shogun remains a pure, distilled expression of what Total War set out to accomplish from the beginning: the fusion of large-scale, turn-based grand strategy with cinematic, real-time battles. Even today, the clarity of its design and the focus of its mechanics give it a unique identity compared to later entries.

Set during Japan’s Sengoku Jidai—the Warring States period—the game casts you as a daimyō vying to unify the islands under a single shogunate. The campaign map is elegantly simple but deeply atmospheric, a parchment-like representation of feudal Japan divided into provinces controlled by rival clans. From this vantage point, you manage taxes, build infrastructure, train armies, conduct diplomacy, and deploy spies and emissaries. Each turn becomes a careful balancing act between economic stability and military expansion. While the management systems are less granular than in later Total War titles, they maintain a tight and purposeful scope that keeps the player focused on strategic positioning, resource flow, and political maneuvering rather than overwhelming micromanagement.

The transition from serene strategic planning to chaotic real-time battles remains one of the game’s greatest strengths. When armies meet, you take direct control of your troops—samurai archers, yari spearmen, cavalry, monks, and more—commanding them across rolling hills, misty forests, and carefully chosen choke points. Terrain plays a critical role, and morale is often more decisive than raw numbers. Units can flee if flanked or if their leader falls, turning the tide in seconds. Small tactical errors have dramatic consequences, which lends battles a sense of weight and authenticity. Despite the game’s age, these clashes still feel gripping, partly because they rely on clear battlefield fundamentals rather than layers of modern system complexity.

Each clan feels distinct thanks to its starting location, advantages, and political landscape. Choosing Takeda means leaning into cavalry dominance; choosing Uesugi provides opportunities for monk warriors and religious influence; selecting Oda gives access to massed ashigaru infantry early on. These asymmetries create natural replay value. Combined with unpredictable AI behavior and shifting alliances, every campaign plays out differently. The Mongol Invasion expansion further refreshes the experience by introducing an external threat from overseas—forcing Japan’s clans to either unite or be overrun by an army built on brute strength and superior ranged weaponry.

However, revisiting Shogun today does highlight its age. The interface is minimalist, sometimes obscure by modern standards. Diplomacy is functional but extremely limited, barely scratching the surface of what later Total War titles would offer. The economy, while intuitive, lacks nuance; once a province has its basic infrastructure, growth becomes predictable. The AI can be opportunistic but also erratic, occasionally making baffling strategic decisions. Visuals, though stylistically appealing, are unmistakably dated, and players accustomed to the spectacle of more recent games may initially find the presentation simplistic. Yet for many, these constraints are part of the game’s enduring charm: the systems may be simple, but they interact cleanly, creating an experience that feels focused rather than reduced.

The History Edition also serves as a preservation effort, ensuring the game runs more reliably on modern machines. While it does not overhaul the graphics or redesign features, the update provides stability improvements, compatibility fixes, and smoother overall performance. For anyone who struggled to run the original digitally, this version offers a frictionless way to return to a formative strategy classic.

Ultimately, Shogun: Total War – Collection remains compelling because of its clarity and elegance. It captures the brutality and beauty of feudal Japan through a design philosophy that values restraint and cohesion. Every decision matters, every battle feels personal, and every campaign tells a rising arc of ambition, betrayal, and conquest. For players who appreciate historical strategy, deliberate pacing, and tactical depth delivered through clean design, Shogun still stands tall. It may lack the complexity of its successors, but what it offers—the foundation of the Total War formula delivered with sharp focus—makes it not just a nostalgic relic, but a timeless entry in strategy gaming.

He jugado este videojuego en cuarentena; durante un año entero. Le tengo un cariño especial. Por lo que le dedicó una reseña como Dios manda para que reciba los méritos que le corresponden. 

Si te gustan los juegos de mesa del estilo T.E.G/RISK es la clase de juego para vos.
La saga de Total war se decantó a la simulación a lo largo de su trayectoria, y si venís buscando eso, vas a terminar odiando este modelo.

En especial sumando lo bruto que nos resulta ahora el choque de controles y técnicas de principio de siglo. Si cumplís ese único requisito o estás acostumbrado a videojuegos viejos no deberías dejarlo de lado. 

La ambientación gracias a la dirección de arte es excelente. Fácilmente engancha en las batallas, cinemáticas, eventos. Lastima que el tiempo hace lo suyo y puede arruinar por lo técnico (Sea resolución, el CGI de época, traducciones, etc.) un trabajo de arte bueno. 

El modelo de tablero/batalla en tiempo real funciona, aunque le falte pulido en detalles, es completamente disfrutable. Carece de re jugabilidad por lo que el mejor consejo es jugar unas pocas campañas largas. 
Las unidades tienen una pequeña función de personalización; que no los detiene de ser peones sin alma pero permite dedicando poco tiempo tener unidades que destacan por méritos fuera de los líderes de facción.

La simulación y viabilidad de tácticas militares es limitada. Es un excelente punto de entrada para practicar lo básico pero con el tiempo encontrás oportunidades o movimientos más delicados y avanzados que no es posible simular.  

Es el inicio de una idea y se le debe tratar con esas expectativas. No es perfecto pero es un buen trabajo.

The Original Gangsta, technologically much simpler than its descendants, but like comfort food it's still satisfying even after all these years. I still have my original install CD from back in the day, and this Steam port is near-identical. 

A combination of board-game style play with a large-scale 3D battlefield combat mode lets you focus on the part of the game you find most appealing. The PS2-era graphics are a bit blocky and low-def (more so in battlefield mode than on the strategy map), but in context still quite good overall. The very dated GUI suffers from repetitive micro-movements and too-many-clicks design (especially by modern standards), but it's not so carpal-tunnel as to be uncomfortably unplayable. 

If your main focus is on commanding an army in battlefield mode, honestly your best choice is Shogun II or later. This original version, while quite good, is very tricky to control effectively due to technical limitations of the time, plus its aforementioned GUI design issues. Where the OG Total War truly shines is on the STRATEGY MAP, which despite the GUI's flaws is still the gold standard IMO. 

The simple color-coded 2D board-game-style map layout is instantly intuitive and clearly readable at a glance (much like the classic board game RISK), with each army represented by a flagged 3D token featuring a generic figure for its commanding officer. Your mounted Daimyo's token is unique (always-on-top when stacked), with each clan naturally only being allowed one Daimyo at any time. The flag itself is a thermometer indicator of that token's total number of soldiers, and is starred with the battle rank of the commander for easy identification of high-value combat units. 

Most tokens stack to a maximum of 16 units, maximum troop numbers per unit can be adjusted in settings and damaged units can be merged to create whole ones, making space for replacements to be added. Some unit types cannot be stacked (Ninja, Shinobi, etc.) which just adds to the GUI's repetitive micro-movements problem, but for the most part it's manageable unless you're dealing with truly large numbers of unstackable tokens. This is mostly an Imagawa Clan problem, TBH. You know, the clan that historically won these wars? 

It's 100% possible to play the game entirely on the strategy map RISK-style via these tokens without ever joining the battles (with the auto-battle dialog), or you can pick and choose which specific combat encounters are worthy of your personal attention. Even if you like to spend most of your time on the battlefield, strategy map manipulation is a huge part of the game. And as you already know if you've played any other titles in this series, sheer numbers alone do not always determine the outcome! 

Respects your time:  Normal difficulty is reasonably challenging, but if you have limited gaming time then an Easy difficulty campaign can often be finished in a single evening. You can also streamline the victory conditions for even tighter time constraints. Just don't get overconfident; all levels of the game's AI are programmed with the Art of War and it rarely lets you forget that. When selecting the difficulty level at game creation, be aware that it jumps significantly with each increase, applying to both game modes. Former pushovers will become much more powerful, resilient and devious with every difficulty increase, and strategy-map-exclusive play becomes increasingly less viable.

Fandom's Total War Wiki has the complete gameplay Manual (with keyboard shortcuts) and the Tech Tree downloadable in PDF at the bottom of the page, both strongly recommended:
https://totalwar.fandom.com/wiki/Shogun:_Total_War

TIP: Using Quicksave (CTRL+S) before committing an action allows you to "undo" with Quickload (CTRL + L) if things go badly. This client port occasionally has an annoying habit of randomly minimizing itself to the desktop, at least on my Windows 11 system (fully patched, updated drivers etc.). If this happens on the battlefield screen, that few moments of downtime can potentially cost you a defeat. SAVE OFTEN!

CHEAT CODES: There are a few (searchable online), IF you want to use them. As a mostly strategy-map player, the only one I've ever had any use for is the strategy map reveal (toggle); the code is actually the name of one of the developers, listed in the endgame credits. The other codes are fun to try once, but they basically ruin the gameplay.  Your mileage may vary.

А от на глобальній карті все порівняно добре. Екран покращень провінції, екран рекрутів, іноді перевірка чисельності гарнізону - от і все що по хорошому вам потрібно. Все інше знаходиться безпосередньо на карті: генерали воюють, шинобі [strike]шиноблять[/strike] шпигують, чи частіше займаються контррозвідкою, дипломати мандрують по карті щоб фідити ворожих ніндзя, а гейші просто дуже приємні особи. 25 years and one month after its release, I still think that out of all "old - school" Total Wars, Shogun: Total War, the game that started them all, is the most interesting and exotic of them.

It shows fully what all "canon" ideas of old TW were, and how it was envisioned, before Rome and Medieval 2: Total War came, and by 'reloading' old concepts in 3D map, started a golden era of series.

From creative crossover between classical wargames (on daimyo's war map), Civilisation and strategies like Risk (but still with taxes dependent on harvest autumns), through simple battles where in low resolutions dead warriors looked like sweet - sour rice bowl spilled over, to spy diplomacy, throne room and college humor assasination videos (with Medieval 2 and Shogun 2 briefly returning to them) - it had it all.

And it is still playable. As well as very enjoyable. And as fresh in taste, as it was quarter a century ago.

Even its bugs and 2,5D Pixel Age graphics were giving hope for better, more advanced future of strategic gaming that Rome and later titles somewhat brought; and nowadays, Shogun: Total War remains a classic of classics and golden foundation of my favourite strategy game series.
